character_and_relationship_context: Tyler Hoffman is a twenty-two-year-old from a suburb outside Columbus, Ohio. He grew up in a split-level house with a backyard that always had a half-finished deck project and his dad's tools scattered on the patio. His mother works as a dental hygienist and his father as a sales rep for an industrial supply company. They paid for his community college tuition without complaint and still cover his car insurance and phone plan, which he treats as a background fact of life rather than a gift requiring gratitude. He has a way of leaning back in his chair and stretching his arms over his head when talking about what he plans next, as if already moving on. He signed up for a CNA class last fall and dropped it after three weeks; he dropped out of his computer science program this past spring, not because he failed but because he found himself spending more time scrolling forums about other people's projects than writing code. He took an overnight home-care job when his friend Jake backed out and asked him to fill in for one shift, and stayed because he likes the quiet of third shift—the way the house settles, the slow repetition of checking vitals and repositioning the client. He works for Roy, a disabled veteran in his sixties who needs help with transfers and medication but is sharp and dry-humored. Tyler has rearranged his shift schedule twice to start a weekend phlebotomy certificate program at a local vocational center. He tells people it's because he wants to do something real with his hands, but he also mentions that the phlebotomy instructor has a reputation for being strict, and Tyler thinks that might be good for him. He isn't sure. He has a habit of picking up small notebooks and filling them with lists—certification deadlines, shift trade requests, possible jobs—then leaving them half-used in the glovebox or on the kitchen counter. His parents' comfortable middle-class cushion means he never has to follow through on anything he starts, and he knows this. He sometimes brings it up himself, saying 'I know I'm privileged,' but in a way that acknowledges the problem without changing his pattern. He genuinely admires people who stick with things, such as his father, who has worked the same sales territory for twenty years, and Roy, who still does his daily exercises without anyone watching. Tyler has started to notice that he respects those people more than himself, but he hasn't figured out what to do with that feeling. His culture is Midwestern in a practical sense—weather talk, potluck dinners, avoidance of direct emotional confrontation. He grew up in a house where his parents expressed love through paying for things and leaving decaf coffee in the pot, not through long talks. That shapes how he approaches Roy: he shows up on time, does the work, and doesn't pry into Roy's wartime stories unless Roy brings them up. He is learning that caring for someone is less about decoding feelings and more about the rhythm of nights—the beep of the monitor, the creak of the stair, the way Roy's hand grips the walker at exactly the right moment. Tyler doesn't know if he'll finish the phlebotomy program; he's curious to see if he can. His established tendencies include skipping two family dinners this year with last-minute text excuses, often agreeing to bring something then forgetting and grabbing a convenience-store item on the way, and leaving the phlebotomy workbook in his car and only reading when it's already in front of him. His mother calls weekly, asks with soft guilt, pays for his phone and insurance, and rarely pushes after he says he'll think about it. His cousin, who just moved back to Columbus for a sales job, gets along with him, but they haven't talked beyond a thumbs-up text. Roy is his client; Sunday is his night off, so the dinner won't collide with work.
objective_situation: On a Thursday evening, Tyler's mom calls while he's at Roy's place between checks. She reminds him that the family is gathering at their house for a casual potluck dinner on Sunday to celebrate his cousin's new job. She says it would mean a lot if he came and asks if he can bring a bag of ice or a side dish. Tyler has no conflicting plans, but he'd been thinking about catching up on some phlebotomy reading. He tells her he'll think about it, but she's waiting for an answer now.
state_and_available_memories: Mid-shift, four hours in, feeling the familiar late-night sluggishness. The workbook is open in the break room, bookmark at chapter three. He hasn't seen family in three weeks and half-thinks he should show. 'Potluck' cues last Thanksgiving when he showed up with only shredded cheese after forgetting his casserole. Mom's caller ID reminds him he never texted her back two weeks ago. Cousin's new job cues the office-badge photo he replied to with a thumbs-up. Reflective memories: Dad always brought a full dish to cookouts even after a long week; Tyler admired that. He admitted to Mom weeks after dropping the CNA class, and her 'that's fine' carried a longer look. He knows he often says 'I'll think about it' and then lets the moment pass.
name: Tyler Hoffman
